traveler: Xul Solar (Oscar Agustin Alejandro Schulz Solari)
title: Lux Reversed: the Twelve Years in Europe, the Invented Tongues, and the House on Laprida
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: San Fernando and the Name Not Yet Taken

stops.name: San Fernando, the birth on the delta edge
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the river town of San Fernando, north of the capital, Oscar Agustin Alejandro Schulz Solari is born to Emilio Schulz Riga, a Baltic German, and Agustina Solari, an Italian of the Ligurian coast. The house speaks more than one language before the child speaks any. Outside the town the Parana is already breaking into the hundred channels of its delta, and none of them is the main one. The registry entry records three given names and two surnames, the Baltic one first; before he is thirty he has replaced the lot with two syllables of his own making.
suggested_refs: Civil registry of San Fernando, Buenos Aires province, birth entry of 14 December 1887
sources: Museo Xul Solar, xulsolar.org.ar, biographical timeline

stops.name: Palermo, the three schools
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources name the schools but not the years of attendance
stops.campa: The boy is sent first to the Colegio Frances Fermy, then to the Colegio Ingles, then to the Colegio Nacional of the northern section at Palermo. Three schools, three languages of instruction, in a Buenos Aires filling with immigrants faster than it can name them. He learns to move between grammars the way other children move between streets. No teacher leaves a record of anything unusual in him; what survives of these years is a list of institutions rather than a portrait of a pupil.
suggested_refs: The Colegio Nacional, Seccion Norte, Palermo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Buenos Aires, architecture abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of enrolment; the abandonment falls about two years later
stops.campa: He enrolls in architecture and leaves after roughly two years, having learned to draw a plan. Nothing takes its place at once. He paints without exhibiting and reads outside every syllabus, in a Buenos Aires of academies and salons that has no category for the work. Later he describes these years from the inside as a sickness with a birth inside it, and puts the crisis in his early twenties. Nothing he paints before 1912 survives, or none of it has been catalogued. He is twenty, and no one has yet found a word for him.
stops.quote: Dazzling light, colors never seen, harmonies of ecstasies and of hell, unheard-of sounds, a new beauty that is mine... If my damaging sorrows are due to labor in childbirth, I am pregnant with an immense, new world!
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, personal writings on the crisis of his early twenties, quoted in Mario H. Gradowczyk, Xul Solar (Buenos Aires: Ediciones ALBA, 1994)
suggested_refs: Gradowczyk's transcription of the early notebooks, describing the pre-1912 crisis

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the ship said Hong Kong
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the fifth of April he boards the England Carrier at the port, working his passage, telling whoever asks that he is bound for Hong Kong and, so the story runs afterward, for a monastic life at the end of it. He is twenty-four. He carries almost nothing and has exhibited nothing. The Rio de la Plata is the color of the land it drains, and the ship goes out across it toward a destination he will not reach. Twelve years pass before he sees this dock again.
suggested_refs: Passenger and crew lists of the England Carrier, April 1912
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'Xul Solar' (names the vessel and the date)
Wikipedia (ES), 'Xul Solar' (Hong Kong intention, no vessel named)

stops.name: Tilbury Docks, the passage abandoned
stops.date_confidence: attested that he disembarks in London in 1912; the specific dock is not documented and Tilbury is given as the era's usual terminus
stops.campa: The passage east ends in the Thames estuary. He disembarks in London and does not reboard. The monastery in Asia becomes, without ceremony, a decade in Europe: no announcement, no letter home explaining the change, only a young man with two surnames walking off a working ship into a city where nobody knows either of them. He goes to the museums and the bookshops. In the British Museum, Assyria and Egypt stand in cases with printed labels, whole scripts kept behind glass and explained to him in a language he is still learning.
suggested_refs: Tilbury Docks, Port of London, standard terminus of the era's long-haul traffic

stops.name: Paris, the first European years
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the sources give a Paris residence in the pre-war years without months
stops.campa: Paris takes him next, and for two years he moves between it and northern Italy without a fixed address in either. He paints small, on paper, in watercolor, because watercolor travels. The city is full of men his age inventing new grammars for painting, and he watches them and joins nothing. Cubism is four years old, the salons argue about it every season, and he exhibits in none of them. What he is doing instead goes into notebooks, in a shorthand nobody else is meant to read.
suggested_refs: The Paris salons and independent exhibitions of 1912 to 1914

stops.name: Turin, the circuit between France and Italy
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Turin is named among his residences without dates
stops.campa: Turin, under its arcades and its hill, becomes one pole of a circuit he keeps walking for years: France, then Italy, then France again. Italy is his mother's country and he speaks it; in the north of it a Schulz Solari can be both foreign names at once and neither of them strange. He supports himself thinly, moves when the money runs out, and paints. No dealer knows him, no catalogue lists him. The years from 1912 to 1918 leave a scatter of city names in the record and very little else.
suggested_refs: The list of European cities Xul Solar later gave as his own itinerary

stops.name: Zoagli, the mother's coast
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the Ligurian base is attested for the war years without a start date
stops.campa: Zoagli on the Ligurian shore is Agustina Solari's town, and her son puts down what passes for roots there, using it as a base between journeys. Genoa is the port down the coast, and he passes through it repeatedly in these years. The war closes borders around him and he keeps crossing them. Nothing he paints here is exhibited, and nothing from these years is dated with confidence; the Ligurian period is known chiefly because he later gave a list of the towns he had lived in, and Zoagli is on it.
suggested_refs: Zoagli, Liguria, native town of Agustina Solari

stops.name: Tours, the war years on the move
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Tours and Marseille are named among the wartime stops without dates
stops.campa: Tours on the Loire, then Marseille on the Mediterranean: the war finds him moving between them, an Argentine with a neutral passport in a Europe that is killing its own generation of painters. He is not conscripted and does not enlist. What he does instead, on paper and in notebooks, is begin the systems: zodiacs, alphabets, correspondences run between number and color and note. Verdun is fought in the years he is settling which planet answers to which vowel. The notebooks carry no address, no publisher and no reader.
suggested_refs: Tours and Marseille among the wartime waystations listed in the English Wikipedia itinerary

stops.name: Florence, Pettoruti and the taking of the name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Spanish account places the name change in Florence, the English gives 1916 without a city
stops.campa: In Florence he meets Emilio Pettoruti, an Argentine painter of his own generation working close to the futurists, and the two recognize each other as the only two of their kind in the city. The friendship holds for the rest of his life. Here he also changes his name: lux, the Latin for light, reversed into Xul, and set beside Solar, which is his mother's surname with a letter taken out. Oscar Schulz Solari signs nothing again. What he does to his own name he will spend forty years doing to language.
stops.quote: [H]e gave himself an extraterrestrial identity by modifying his parents' surnames and becoming Xul Solar. The first name reflected light, or lux, spelled backwards; the last, his maternal surname without the 'i,' was the sun itself.
stops.quote_source: Caleb Bach, "Stairways to the Sun," Americas, vol. 46, no. 1 (Jan-Feb 1994), pp. 6-13
suggested_refs: The first works signed Xul Solar, Florence, 1916
sources: Caleb Bach, 'Stairways to the Sun', Americas (1994)

segments.name: The Consulate, the Workshops, the First Rooms

stops.name: Milan, the Argentine consulate
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of arrival; the post runs about a year and a half
stops.campa: Toward the end of the war he takes a post at the Argentine consulate in Milan and holds it roughly a year and a half, the longest he has stayed anywhere since leaving Buenos Aires. A consulate in wartime is the place where paper decides whether a person may move, and he issues the paper. In the same months he is filling notebooks with signs of his own devising, meant one day to be legible to anyone born anywhere. Milan sees only the clerk, a courteous Argentine with a German surname and an Italian one, working through the last winter of the war.
suggested_refs: Consular staff records of the Argentine consulate at Milan, 1918-1919

stops.name: London, six months out of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested; the stay runs November 1919 to May 1920
stops.campa: He crosses back to London in November and stays until May, six months in the city where his voyage east broke off seven years before. He arrives in a capital just out of a war, cheap and grey and full of museum rooms holding Assyria and Egypt behind glass. He is thirty-two and has still exhibited nothing anywhere. The Milan show that will make him briefly a public artist is already being arranged across the Channel, and he goes back over the water in the spring to hang it.
suggested_refs: The British Museum galleries of the immediate post-war years

stops.name: Galleria Arte, Milan, the first exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested; the show runs 27 November to 16 December 1920
stops.campa: His first show opens in Milan in the last weeks of 1920, shared with the sculptor Arturo Martini. He is thirty-three, eight years out of Buenos Aires, and this is the first time anyone can walk into a room and see what he has been making: small watercolors of flags and ladders and staircases, figures built out of banners, cities built out of writing. Italy looks politely and moves on. He has become, on paper, an artist with a record, which is what he needed before he could go home.
suggested_refs: Exhibition notices for Xul Solar and Arturo Martini, Milan, winter 1920

stops.name: Munich, the work of Paul Klee
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the Munich residence runs to December 1923
stops.campa: He settles in Munich until the December of 1923, through the inflation years, attending art workshops and looking hard at the work of Paul Klee. Nothing in the record puts the two men in a room together; what the sources say is that the Argentine sees the paintings. He recognizes a fellow builder of small, bright, legible worlds, a man who also thinks a picture can be a diagram and a joke at once. Klee's line goes into him and comes out speaking Spanish, or something adjacent to Spanish.
suggested_refs: Munich exhibitions and workshops of 1921 to 1923 showing Klee's work
sources: Fernando Demaria, 'Xul Solar y Paul Klee', Lyra (1971)

stops.name: Stuttgart, hearing Rudolf Steiner
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He travels to Stuttgart to hear Rudolf Steiner lecture. Anthroposophy joins the astrology already running through his notebooks, and joins it without displacing anything, because he is a man who adds systems rather than choosing among them. Steiner's claim that spiritual perception can be trained the way arithmetic is trained is the claim Xul Solar has been acting on for a decade without a doctrine to name it. He takes what he wants from the lectures and leaves the movement alone.
suggested_refs: Rudolf Steiner's Stuttgart lecture cycles of 1923

stops.name: Paris, Aleister Crowley and Leah Hirsig
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the English account places the meeting in Paris in 1924 with Leah Hirsig, the Spanish account places it in 1914, and neither cites a document
stops.campa: In Paris, in the months before he sails for home, he meets Aleister Crowley, then living with Leah Hirsig, and the two occultists talk. One version holds that Crowley shows him a way of taking visions through the I Ching, the book that produces the San Signos six years later. The other version puts the meeting a full decade earlier, and no document has been produced for either. What is certain is that the hexagrams enter his practice and never leave it again.
suggested_refs: Crowley's Paris diaries of 1924, and the Spanish Wikipedia claim of a 1914 meeting

stops.name: Musee Galliera, Paris, the Latin American show
stops.date_confidence: attested; the exhibition runs 15 March to 15 April 1924
stops.campa: His work hangs in the Exposition d'Art Americain-Latin at the Musee Galliera from the middle of March to the middle of April, among painters from a continent that Paris files under a single heading. It is his last public appearance in Europe. Twelve years of walking between Turin and Zoagli and Munich end in a group show of Latin Americans in a French museum. Two months later he books a passage out of Hamburg. The language he is building has no speakers in this city, and none anywhere else either.
suggested_refs: Catalogue of the Exposition d'Art Americain-Latin, Musee Galliera, spring 1924

stops.name: Hamburg, the crossing home
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In June he boards at Hamburg with Emilio Pettoruti, whom he met in Florence eight years earlier, the two of them going back to a country neither has worked in as an adult. He is thirty-six. Twelve years in Europe have produced a dozen addresses and one exhibition held under his own name. He carries home a case of watercolors, a name he invented, and a language with one speaker. The Germany he sails from has just come through the year its currency died and is already arguing about who lost the war.
suggested_refs: Hamburg passenger manifests, June 1924

segments.name: The Return and the Florida Group

stops.name: Port of Buenos Aires, the return after twelve years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; one geographic account wrongly gives June, which is the month of departure from Hamburg
stops.campa: He disembarks in July, twelve years after the England Carrier took him out of this same port. The city has doubled and does not remember him. Within months he is inside the vanguardista circle that meets on Calle Florida and prints Martin Fierro, the Florida group. The young men there have read about the European vanguard; he has stood in front of it for twelve years, and the difference is understood within a week. He is thirty-six and has never yet hung a painting in his own country.
suggested_refs: The Martin Fierro circle of Calle Florida, Buenos Aires, 1924

stops.name: Buenos Aires, meeting Jorge Luis Borges
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the sources place the meeting within the year of his return without a month
stops.campa: He meets Jorge Luis Borges, twelve years younger and just back from his own European decade, and each recognizes what the other is. They read Blake and Swedenborg the same way, as reporters rather than poets, and they agree that a language is a made thing and can therefore be remade. What they talk about for the next thirty-nine years is duodecimal arithmetic, invented tongues and what a reformed universe would require. It is the closest friendship either man has. Borges calls him one of the most singular men of his era and means it as a description.
stops.quote: Xul took on the task of reforming the universe, of proposing on this earth a different order. For that, among other things, he changed the current numerical system of mathematics to use a duodecimal system, with which he painted his watercolors.
stops.quote_source: Jorge Luis Borges, quoted in Cecilia Vicuna, "Co ecos Astri: Xul Solar of Buenos Aires," Words Without Borders, 1 February 2004, trans. Suzanne Jill Levine
suggested_refs: Borges's published recollections of Xul Solar
sources: Cecilia Vicuna, 'Co ecos Astri', Words Without Borders (2004)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the article in Martin Fierro
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He writes in Martin Fierro for Pettoruti's first Buenos Aires exhibition, defending a painting the local press has just finished calling an insult. The argument is that the disorder of the new art is only apparent, that a hard drive toward clear structure runs underneath it, and it closes by setting the whole quarrel inside a larger one: the wars of independence for this America are not yet over. He has been home four months and has already told the country what he thinks it is for.
stops.quote: Although this is a time when art is more individual and arbitrary than ever, it would be a mistake to call it anarchic. In spite of so much confusion, there exists a well-defined tendency toward simplicity of means, toward clear and solid architecture, toward the pure plastic sense that protects and accents abstract meanings of line, mass, and color, all within a complete liberty of subject and composition... Because the wars of independence for our America are not yet over...
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, article for Emilio Pettoruti's first Buenos Aires exhibition, Martin Fierro, 9 October 1924
suggested_refs: Martin Fierro, issue of 9 October 1924
sources: Martin Fierro (1924), reproduced in the Xul Solar literature

stops.name: Galeria Witcomb, the Primer Salon Libre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In December he shows in Argentina for the first time, at the Galeria Witcomb on Calle Florida, in the Primer Salon Libre. The watercolors are small and they are unlike anything on the street outside: flagged cities, serpents made of script, figures climbing ladders between planets, the whole palette lit as if from behind. Buenos Aires cannot tell whether it is looking at painting, at diagram or at scripture. The confusion turns out to be permanent, and he does nothing whatever to relieve it.
suggested_refs: The Galeria Witcomb, Calle Florida, and the Primer Salon Libre of December 1924

stops.name: Amigos del Arte, the modern painters
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He hangs with Norah Borges and Emilio Pettoruti in the Exposicion de Pintores Modernos at Amigos del Arte on Florida, three painters who between them bring most of the European vanguard into Argentine rooms. Marinetti passes through Buenos Aires the same season, futurism arriving in person in a city already arguing about it. Norah Borges is his friend's sister, a painter working inside the same circle and hanging on the same wall. Xul Solar is now a fixture of the modern faction, which does not mean that the watercolors sell.
suggested_refs: Asociacion Amigos del Arte, Florida 659, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Laprida 1212, the house acquired
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the Spanish source gives the number as 1214 and the museum's own address is 1212
stops.campa: In November the family acquires the house at Laprida 1212 in Barrio Norte, and it becomes the workshop of the rest of his life. He rebuilds it around the work: shelves for a library that will reach three and a half thousand volumes, walls for the watercolors, floor space for the boards and the charts. Visitors climb a stair into rooms where the furniture and the paintings are equally his own design. He invents everything that follows inside these rooms, and most of it never leaves them.
suggested_refs: The house at Laprida 1212, Barrio Norte, later the Museo Xul Solar

stops.name: Amigos del Arte, sixty-two works
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Sixty-two works go up at Amigos del Arte in May, the largest showing he has had anywhere. What the critics walk into is Drago and its relatives: watercolors in which snakes carry cities on their backs, staircases climb into zodiacs, and every surface is inscribed with something meant to be read. The vocabulary answers to no school in Paris or Milan any longer. He is forty-one and no longer a young man who traveled; he is the strangest painter in Argentina, and the position is uncontested.
suggested_refs: Catalogue of the Xul Solar exhibition at Amigos del Arte, May 1929

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the San Signos completed
stops.date_confidence: attested to mid-1930
stops.campa: By the middle of 1930 he finishes writing out the San Signos, the record of visions worked through the sixty-four hexagrams of the I Ching and set down largely in neocriollo. It is not a book he tries to publish. It is a document produced by a procedure, in the way an astrological chart is produced by a procedure, and he keeps it as an instrument keeps its readings. The visions have a method behind them, and the method is the point he never gets across to anyone outside the house.
suggested_refs: The San Signos manuscript, held by the Fundacion Pan Klub

stops.name: Buenos Aires, neocriollo in print
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He begins publishing neocriollo in Argentine magazines, which is to say he begins asking readers to read a language with exactly one fluent speaker. Portuguese vowels open Spanish words, particles are invented wherever the two tongues disagree, and the result is legible at a glance and impossible to translate cleanly. He speaks it aloud to friends in the house on Laprida, and expects to be answered. Borges, who loves it, is among the very few who can follow him at speed, and the magazines print the texts without a glossary because no glossary exists.
stops.quote: Olas, ólitas, vintos, hálitos, réspiras, kinflores, hondónadas, pirmanchas, kingramas, biovacíos, tunzoes: too fon.
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, Pan Criollo, quoted in Cecilia Vicuna, "Co ecos Astri: Xul Solar of Buenos Aires," Words Without Borders, trans. Suzanne Jill Levine
suggested_refs: Xul Solar's neocriollo texts in the Argentine little magazines of the 1930s
sources: Cecilia Vicuna, 'Co ecos Astri', Words Without Borders (2004)

stops.name: Laprida 1212, the Pan Klub opens
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He opens the Pan Klub in the house: a salon and workshop where astrology, painting, invented scripts, modified games and the drawing of charts are one occupation carried on by one set of people. He is casting horoscopes now for anyone who asks. Among the objects in circulation is a tarot of his own making, the deck rebuilt for reading rather than play, a form Etteilla first cut out of the ordinary playing pack in Paris a century and a half before. The club outlasts him by decades.
stops.quote: I am maestro of a writing no one reads yet.
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, quoted in Cecilia Vicuna, "Co ecos Astri: Xul Solar of Buenos Aires," Words Without Borders, 2004, trans. Suzanne Jill Levine
suggested_refs: The Pan Klub rooms at Laprida 1212, still operating inside the museum

segments.name: The War Years and the Pan-Games

stops.name: Buenos Aires, named inside Tlon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Borges publishes Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius, in which a planet's languages are described in detail, and names Xul Solar inside the story as the man who renders its sentences. Xul Solar traduce con brevedad, the text says. The joke is not a joke: his friend is the only person in Buenos Aires who manufactures languages by trade, and a story about an invented world needs a translator who exists. The fiction borrows a real inventor and puts him in undisguised.
suggested_refs: Jorge Luis Borges, 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius' (1940)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the monochrome years
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year the phase begins
stops.campa: His painting goes monochrome. The flagged and lettered cities give way to work in a single register, thinner and colder, made while Europe burns again three thousand miles off and Argentine neutrality holds. A later critic will say he reached his highest expressive point in these ascetic pictures and will tie their theme to the anguish of the moment. He writes nothing about the war. The pictures carry it, in a palette drained of the light his name is made from.
stops.quote: Xul reached his highest point of artistic expressivity in these ascetic paintings whose theme corresponded to that anguishing reality
stops.quote_source: Mario H. Gradowczyk, Xul Solar (Buenos Aires: Ediciones ALBA, 1994), on the 1943-1944 paintings including Fiordo
suggested_refs: Fiordo and the monochrome works of 1941 to 1944

stops.name: Rosario, astrology from a public platform
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; reported by the Spanish Wikipedia without a primary citation
stops.campa: He goes up the Parana to Rosario to lecture on astrology, taking onto a public platform a practice most of his contemporaries treat as a parlor amusement. For him it has rules and a procedure, and it settles which colors go into a painting as surely as it settles what a client should be told. The Rosario audience gets the entire system rather than the entertaining half of it. No text of the lecture survives, and the single account that reports the trip cites nothing.
suggested_refs: Notices of Xul Solar's Rosario astrology lecture, 1943

stops.name: Buenos Aires, three hundred copies for Borges and Bioy
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He illustrates Un modelo para la muerte, a detective novel written jointly by Borges and Adolfo Bioy Casares under the single invented name B. Suarez Lynch, in an edition of three hundred copies. Two men who invent an author, illustrated by a man who invented himself. The book is not sold; the copies go to friends. It is the distribution his own alphabets and games have had for twenty years, and he is the last man in the city who would find that strange.
suggested_refs: B. Suarez Lynch, Un modelo para la muerte (1944), illustrated edition of 300 copies

stops.name: Buenos Aires, panajedrez and the pan-games
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the games are dated to about 1945 and the board's dimensions are given differently by different sources
stops.campa: He builds panajedrez, a chess on an enlarged board where each move also composes music, poetry and an astrological figure, so that a single game yields several artifacts at once. He builds a marionette I Ching, a piano notation meant to cut study to a third of the usual time, a duodecimal arithmetic he paints in. Nobody plays these things except him and his circle. He describes himself, with complete accuracy, as world champion of a game that nobody yet knows.
stops.quote: I am a world champion of a game that nobody yet knows called panchess (Panajedrez). I am master of a script that nobody yet reads. I am creator of a technique, of a musical grafia that allows the piano to be studied in a third of the usual time that it takes today. I am director of a theatre that as yet has not begun working. I am creator of a universal language called panlingua based on numbers and astrology that will help people know each other better. I am creator of twelve painting techniques...
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, from his own writings, reproduced in the Quotes section of the English Wikipedia article 'Xul Solar'
suggested_refs: The Pan Game and Marionette I Ching, a copy of which is held by the Museum of Modern Art, New York

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the marriage to Lita Cadenas
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of August he marries Micaela Cadenas, called Lita, whom he has known from the astrological gatherings for about ten years. He is fifty-eight and she is forty-four, though the Spanish account, doing its arithmetic on a December birthday, ages him by a year. The household on Laprida now holds two people who read charts. She will outlive him by decades and spend them turning the house into the institution that keeps the paintings, the library and the games together.
suggested_refs: Marriage register, Buenos Aires, 13 August 1946

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the manifesto in the magazine El
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He writes for the magazine El a plain account of his own inventions: neocriollo, the panlengua built on number and astrology and music, panajedrez, the notations, the games. It is a manifesto in the form of an inventory, written by a man of sixty who has spent thirty years making instruments for a civilization that has not arrived. He calls the whole effort patriotism, and by patriotism he means finding the highest ideal available to human beings and spreading it over the entire world.
stops.quote: Our patriotism is finding the highest possible ideal of humanity-fulfilling and spreading it all over the world
stops.quote_source: Xul Solar, quoted in Cecilia Vicuna, "Co ecos Astri: Xul Solar of Buenos Aires," Words Without Borders, trans. Suzanne Jill Levine
suggested_refs: The 1947 manifesto in the magazine El
sources: Cecilia Vicuna, 'Co ecos Astri', Words Without Borders (2004)

segments.name: Li-Tao, the House on the Water

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the kabbalah paintings
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year the series begins; it runs to the middle of the decade
stops.campa: From 1951 into the middle of the decade he paints the kabbalah: the sefirot, the letters, the ladders of ascent, rendered in the same bright legible hand that drew the flags and the cities. Hebrew joins the alphabets already at work in the house. He is not converting to anything. He is doing what he has done since Florence, taking a system that claims the world is written and treating the claim as a working instruction for a painter. The paintings are small and the ambition in them is not.
suggested_refs: The kabbalah series of 1951 onward, Museo Xul Solar

stops.name: Villa La Nata, the house named Li-Tao
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He buys a house on the Rio Lujan at Villa La Nata, in the delta above Buenos Aires, and names it Li-Tao. The delta is a country of channels and willows and wooden houses standing on stilts, reached by launch, an hour and a world away from Barrio Norte. A man who spent his life fusing Spanish with Portuguese and Latin with Chinese names his retreat in two syllables that could come from the I Ching or from nowhere at all, and does not say which. He is sixty-six.
suggested_refs: Li-Tao, the Xul Solar house at Villa La Nata, Dique Lujan, partido de Tigre

stops.name: Villa La Nata, the move to the delta
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the permanent move is reported without documentary support
stops.campa: He moves out to the delta for good, with the Laprida house behind him. The last years are spent on the water: charts, kabbalah, the pan-games, visitors arriving by boat. Buenos Aires has by now half-accepted him as a national eccentric, a category that costs the city nothing and explains nothing. On the river he is simply a man of seventy working every day inside a system he has been extending since 1912 and has never once called finished. The water goes past the stilts of the house in both directions, according to the tide.
suggested_refs: The delta of the Rio Lujan, Tigre, in the 1950s

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the certificate of spiritual baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested; the document is a Certificado de Bautizo Espiritual, not, as sometimes stated, a kriya yoga initiation
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of May a certificate of spiritual baptism is issued to him in the manner of the Self-Realization Fellowship, the yoga lineage carried west out of Bengal. At seventy-two he is still adding: the practice set beside the hexagrams, the horoscopes, the sefirot and the anthroposophy, none of them cancelling any other. The ship he boarded in 1912 had Hong Kong on its papers and he never arrived. The Asia he wanted reached him instead, by post, in the form of a document.
suggested_refs: Certificado de Bautizo Espiritual, 15 May 1960, in the Fundacion Pan Klub archive

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the work crosses a border
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Work of his is exhibited in Rio de Janeiro in July. Brazil is the other half of the language he built; neocriollo exists precisely because he held that the continent's two tongues were one tongue that had been allowed to drift. The watercolors go north to the country whose vowels he had been folding into Spanish for thirty years, sent by a man of seventy-three who no longer travels. No source consulted records whether anyone in Rio noticed that the paintings were, in their own way, addressed to them.
suggested_refs: The 1961 Rio de Janeiro exhibition including work by Xul Solar

stops.name: Palais de Tokyo, Paris, Art argentin actuel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the show is a group exhibition of current Argentine art, not the retrospective some accounts describe
stops.campa: Paris shows him again at the Musee National d'Art Moderne, then housed in the Palais de Tokyo, in a group exhibition of current Argentine art. Thirty-eight years after his last European appearance he returns to the same city as one name among many, sent by a country rather than carried there by himself. He does not travel to it. He is seventy-four and living on the delta, and the paintings make the crossing without him, which is the reverse of every earlier trip he took.
suggested_refs: Art argentin actuel, Musee National d'Art Moderne, Palais de Tokyo, Paris, 1962

stops.name: Villa La Nata, the rosary of seventy-one beads
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies at Li-Tao on the ninth of April, seventy-five years old, Lita at his side, holding in his hands a wooden rosary of seventy-one carved beads. Nothing in his life ever ran on one system alone, and the last object in it is a counting device from a religion he never confined himself to, carrying a number that no source explains. Borges gives the eulogy. No source consulted names the cemetery or the grave, which stays a gap in the record of a man who mapped the heavens.
suggested_refs: The wooden rosary of seventy-one beads, reported in the Spanish account of his death

segments.name: The Rooms Kept As He Left Them

stops.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, ninety-three works
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: Six months after his death the national museum hangs ninety-three of his works as Homenaje a Xul Solar, with a prologue written by Borges. The friend who called him one of the most singular men of his era writes the introduction to the room where the country finally sees all of it at once: the flagged cities, the alphabets, the zodiacs, the monochromes of the war years. It is the first time the whole apparatus stands visible to people who never climbed the stairs on Laprida.
suggested_refs: Homenaje a Xul Solar (1887-1963), Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, October 1963, prologue by Borges

stops.name: Laprida 1212, the museum opens
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of May the Museo Xul Solar opens in the Laprida house, thirty years after his death, made by Lita Cadenas and the Fundacion Pan Klub she built to hold it. The library of some three thousand five hundred volumes stays on its shelves, the paintings on the walls, the invented alphabets and the modified games in their cases, and the Pan Klub goes on meeting under its own old name, in the house where he coined it. The foundation holds the rights to every image he made. He arranged the rooms; she kept them arranged.
suggested_refs: Museo Xul Solar, Fundacion Pan Klub, Laprida 1212, Buenos Aires, opened 13 May 1993
